lines.speaker: Philip
lines.text: Now, Alexander, you wouldn't deny you're my son. If you were Ammon's, you wouldn't have died.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: I knew I was Philip son of Amyntas, father. But I took the oracle because it seemed useful for my plans.

lines.speaker: Philip
lines.text: What? Useful to let yourself be fooled by prophets?

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: No, but the barbarians were terrified of me, thinking they were fighting a god. No one resisted anymore, so I conquered them more easily.

lines.speaker: Philip
lines.text: And what worthy opponents did you conquer? You always faced cowards with their little bows, little shields, and wicker barriers. Conquering Greeks—that would have been something. The Boeotians, Phocians, Athenians, the Arcadian hoplites, the Thessalian cavalry, the Eleian javelin-men, the Mantinean peltasts, or even the Thracians, Illyrians, Paeonians. Those are real feats. But Medes, Persians, Chaldeans—soft, gold-wearing men. Don't you know that before you, the Ten Thousand with Clearchus marched up and beat them without even coming to close quarters? They ran before the arrows could reach.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: But the Scythians, father, and the Indian elephants—that wasn't nothing. And I beat them without splitting their forces or buying victories with betrayals. I never broke an oath, lied in a promise, or did anything dishonorable just to win. And the Greeks—some I took without bloodshed, but the Thebans... you must have heard how I dealt with them.

lines.speaker: Philip
lines.text: I know all that. Cleitus told me—the one you ran through with your spear at dinner because he dared praise me over your achievements.

lines.speaker: Philip
lines.text: And you threw off the Macedonian cloak and put on a Persian robe, they say, and stuck an upright tiara on your head, expecting Macedonians—free men—to prostrate themselves before you. Most ridiculous of all, you copied the ways of the people you'd beaten. I won't even mention the rest: locking learned men up with lions, those marriages of yours, your excessive love for Hephaestion. The one thing I praised when I heard it was that you left Darius's wife alone, even though she was beautiful, and looked after his mother and daughters. That was kingly.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: And my love of danger, father? Don't you praise that? Leaping first over the wall at the Oxydracae and taking all those wounds?

lines.speaker: Philip
lines.text: I don't praise it, Alexander—not because I think it's wrong for a king to get wounded or lead from the front. But it did you no good. If people thought you were a god, and then they saw you carried off the field on a stretcher, bleeding and groaning from the wound, that was a joke to everyone watching. It exposed Ammon as a fraud and the prophets as flatterers. Who wouldn't laugh at the son of Zeus fainting and begging doctors for help? Now that you're dead, don't you think plenty of people are mocking that whole pretense, watching the god's corpse lying there rotting and bloated like any other body? And that 'useful' thing you mentioned—conquering easily because of it—actually robbed your victories of their glory. Everything looked like it was done by a god who couldn't quite manage it.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: That's not what people think of me. They set me alongside Heracles and Dionysus. And that Rock of Aornus that neither of them could take—I took it alone.

lines.speaker: Philip
lines.text: You see? You're talking like Ammon's son again, comparing yourself to Heracles and Dionysus. Aren't you ashamed, Alexander? Won't you drop the vanity now, know yourself, and understand—now that you're dead?
